speaker_summary: Ashraf Ahmed, former president of the Dhaka Chamber, arguing steadily against the change. He accepts that around seventy percent of countries run January to December and that Bangladesh's calendar is not unusual, but says the private sector gets no economic benefit from moving it and carries a real economic cost. His central question is proportion: government is ten to fifteen percent of the economy and the private sector is the other eighty-five, so imposing this cost on the eighty-five for the state's convenience needs justifying. He dismantles the stated rationale - everyone already knows the monsoon falls in July to September, so seasonality is adjusted in planning, and the DPP system already requires monthly and quarterly plans, so nothing changes by moving the calendar. On the transition he itemises the cost: a nine-month reporting period means extra staff, reworked books, and recalculation of withholding tax and VAT that are all computed on twelve months. His repeated complaint is that no assessment was done and nobody asked the private sector.
speaker_rationale: All five turns are unfavourable and three are severe. He is measured in register but unequivocal in substance, and ends saying he still has no answer to why it is being done in a hurry.

speaker_summary: Dr Mahfuz Kabir, an economist, giving the more sympathetic reading while still landing unfavourably. He accepts the government's stated case - the fiscal year currently opens in July as the disaster season begins, so the country builds and loses in the same months, and there is a cycle in which contractors and project administrators share what that waste generates while public money disappears. He allows a real gain if money is disbursed at the start of the year and the first three months are usable. Against that he lists what the change actually requires: every statistical series from BBS through Bangladesh Bank's financial sector data to the stock market recalculated, a serious work plan, extra manpower and substantial investment, and extra pressure on firms that are closed or only just reopening through incentive packages. His conclusion is that the change will have far-reaching effects across every sector and that the private sector currently feels fear rather than benefit.
speaker_rationale: Six unfavourable turns against none favourable, with two neutral. He states the government's rationale fairly and identifies genuine advantages, which keeps this well short of his co-panellist.

speaker_summary: Rezaul Karim Roni, an editor who was in the prime minister's three-hour meeting with businessmen and media that day and reports it from inside. His central distinction is that the government has no planning problem - the manifesto shows that - but an implementation problem, and the real challenge is executing any plan inside a fragile economic structure. He describes what was presented: a day-by-day practical picture running to 2031, a clear road map combining coal, furnace oil and solar, a one-stop service centre for phantom bills, and smart prepaid meters. He reports the government's own answer on ending meter charges - that it would cost twenty-nine to thirty-four thousand crore taka in extra subsidy it cannot presently afford, though it plans to phase it. He notes Bangladesh's fuel price increase was the lowest in South Asia and that prices remain comparatively low, while conceding that recovery means returning to a position that was itself fragile and that villages bear far more load shedding than cities.
speaker_rationale: Six favourable turns against three unfavourable, with eight neutral turns on the corruption inquiry where he argues for a professional rather than politically biased investigation. He is reporting a government plan approvingly while stating its limits, which makes him favourable overall rather than mixed.
